title: Slot Insert
statement: A shared calendar stores reserved slots as [start, end] pairs in slots, sorted by start and pairwise disjoint (each slot ends before the next one starts). Both endpoints are included, so [1, 3] and [3, 5] would share minute 3. Insert newSlot and return the calendar as a sorted list of disjoint slots, merging newSlot with every slot it shares at least one minute with.

examples.explanation: [6, 10] overlaps [5, 7] and [9, 12], so the three become [5, 12].
[4, 6] touches nothing and is placed between the existing slots.

hints.content: The existing slots are already sorted and disjoint; you do not need to sort anything.
Every slot falls into one of three groups: entirely before newSlot, overlapping it, or entirely after it.
A slot is entirely before newSlot when its end is smaller than newSlot's start. A slot overlaps when its start is at most newSlot's current end.
Copy the 'before' slots, then grow newSlot to absorb each overlapping slot by taking the smaller start and the larger end.
After absorbing, push the grown slot once and copy the remaining slots unchanged. That is a single linear pass.

testCases.explanation: [6, 10] overlaps [5, 7] and [9, 12], so the three become [5, 12].
[4, 6] touches nothing and is placed between the existing slots.
An empty calendar gains one slot.
Sharing minute 3 merges the slots into [1, 5].
The new slot comes before everything.
The new slot comes after everything.
The new slot swallows the whole calendar.
A slot inside an existing slot changes nothing.
Negative times work the same way: [-5, -3] merges with [-3, -1].

solutions.title: Append, sort and merge
solutions.intuition: Inserting and re-merging from scratch is the general interval-merge routine, which is always correct.
solutions.approach: Append newSlot to a copy of slots, sort by start, then sweep and merge any slot whose start is at most the previous block's end.
solutions.pseudocode:
all = slots + [newSlot]; sort by start; merged = []
for (s, e) in all: if merged and s <= last.end: last.end = max(last.end, e) else push [s, e]
return merged
commonMistakes: Using s < last.end, which keeps touching slots separate.
Mutating the caller's slot arrays while merging.
solutions.interviewExplanation: This reuses the standard merge sweep. It ignores that the input is already sorted, so it pays for a sort that is not needed.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: [5,7] and [6,10] merge into [5,10], which then merges with [9,12] into [5,12].

solutions.title: Three-phase linear scan
solutions.intuition: Because the calendar is sorted and disjoint, the slots that interact with newSlot form one contiguous run.
solutions.approach: Copy slots that end before newSlot starts. Then, while the next slot starts at or before the growing slot's end, absorb it. Push the grown slot, then copy the rest.
solutions.pseudocode:
i = 0; out = []
while i < n and slots[i].end < start: out.push(slots[i++])
while i < n and slots[i].start <= end: start = min(start, slots[i].start); end = max(end, slots[i].end); i++
out.push([start, end]); copy remaining
return out
commonMistakes: Forgetting the final copy loop, which drops every slot after the merge.
Comparing with the original newSlot end instead of the grown end, which misses chains of overlaps.
solutions.interviewExplanation: The input is sorted and disjoint, so the slots touching newSlot form one contiguous run. I copy everything that ends before it, absorb the run by widening start and end, emit the merged slot, and copy the tail. It's one pass, O(n), and it never mutates the input.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: [5,7] starts at 5 <= 10, so the slot grows to [5,10]; [9,12] starts at 9 <= 10, so it grows to [5,12].
